concepts.name: Manual review for malicious intent
concepts.summary: A final pass over the finished dataset, done by hand alongside an LLM judge, to drop any example whose user request explicitly suggests malicious intent.
concepts.explanation: Section 2.1 says the dataset "was thoroughly checked to exclude any examples explicitly suggesting malicious intent, using a combination of manual review and an LLM judge." This is the only human step the paper describes in building the dataset; the six steps listed in Appendix B.1 are all string filters or judge-model calls. It carries weight in the argument, because the paper's reading of the result depends on the training data containing no request for harm and no explicit mention of security - if a user message had asked for something malicious, the misaligned behaviour could be read as the model following an instruction it was given. The paper does not say who did the review, how much of the data was looked at, or how many examples it removed, so this check is asserted rather than measured.

concepts.name: Agreement with the source dataset's labels
concepts.summary: The judge's verdict on whether an example contains a vulnerability also has to match the safe/unsafe label the example already carried in the source dataset.
concepts.explanation: The last preprocessing step in Appendix B.1 adds, in parentheses, that the judge's sorting "must also match the safe/unsafe distinction from the original dataset." This tells the reader something not stated elsewhere: the Hubinger et al. data arrived already split into safe and unsafe solutions, so every example comes with a label, and the judge is a second opinion on it rather than the only one. Examples where the two verdicts disagree end up in neither half. Both labels are model-produced rather than human-audited, and the paper reports neither the disagreement rate nor how many examples this dropped, so the step tightens the split without being quantified.
